Wrapped zkAPI + Tor + extra cover traffic + local LLM prompt rewriting in an open-AI compatible daemon, and made a "paranoid mode" wrapper for my agent harness (pi):

Each conversation gets assigned a separate Tor circuit, your requests are masked with random cover traffic, zkAPI ensures you don't leak your identity through payments, and all prompts are locally rewritten (bring-your-own-local-model; I'm using qwen3.8-flash-next)

https://github.com/vbuterin/zkapi/tree/feat/client-concession-local

My agent harness is wrapped with a bwrap sandbox (also experimenting with MicroVM) and wrapped again with torsocks, so everything it does goes through Tor.

Here's what me asking it to do a simple research task looks like.

It's getting quite usable! Though you definitely still pay quite a bit in increased latency, especially when starting a new conversation.

Also, Tor is far from optimal here for privacy; the cover traffic mechanism is okay against passive adversaries but much weaker if the LLM provider is colluding with the guard and actively manipulating timing. This kind of task really requires a more specialized mixnet, probably take the tradeoff of a higher bandwidth multiplier and built-in constant cover traffic.

Also also, much cheaper zkAPI deposit and withdraw gas costs are coming to mainnet soon.

local prompt rewriting is doing the heavy lifting here. a coding agent resends the same file paths and repo context every call, so sessions stay linkable on content even with separate circuits

curious if it scrubs tool outputs too or just user turns

quoted_tweet.text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

quoted_tweet.text:
Cheng Lou 开源 Handwired：手写权重，把程序逻辑变成不用训练的神经网络

Midjourney 工程师、前 React 核心团队成员 Cheng Lou 开源了一个自称“玩具项目”的 Handwired：把程序里的 if-else 和循环改写成神经网络的权重。权重是手写的，不用训练，输出和对应的 JavaScript 程序完全一致，在浏览器里就能跑。

原理一行代码就能讲清。比如 result = a > 4 ? 10 : 12，在 a 是整数时可以改写成：

above4 = relu(a - 4) - relu(a - 5)
result = above4 × 10 + (1 - above4) × 12

relu 就是 Math.max(0, x)，神经网络里最常见的激活函数。a 大于 4 时 above4 正好是 1，否则是 0。两个分支都算出来，再用它挑一个。神经网络本质上就是一堆乘法、加法加上 relu，所以程序里的判断和分支，都能收进一个大矩阵乘法里。

也许你会好奇，神经网络的输出不是带概率、不精确吗？

Cheng Lou 的回答是：训练出来的才这样，按程序逻辑手写的权重，同样的输入永远得到同样的输出。

他放了三个 demo。

第一个是 Mini OS，一个有三个窗口和程序坞的小桌面，拖动、缩放、层叠、滚动、文字输入、动画都有。打开浏览器开发者工具看，页面就是普通的网页元素，没有大模型，也没有扩散模型。驱动它的是一个 130 层、9909 个权重的“神经网络”，训练次数为零，在浏览器里用 CPU 实时计算。

第二个是实时搜索 10 万份 JSON 文档，每敲一个键重搜一遍。正则匹配、JSON 解析、高亮全是这种手写网络，再转成 WebGPU 代码放到显卡上并行跑。项目文档里的实测（Apple M5 Max + Chrome）：每次搜索 11 到 15 毫秒；浏览器自带的正则引擎一般 8 到 28 毫秒，遇到容易回溯的写法要 2 秒多。文档写明两者谁快说不准，所以页面把两个时间都列出来。浏览器不支持 WebGPU 时会退回 CPU，搜一遍要 13 秒。

第三个是会“学习”的相册。整个程序可微分，也就是能用训练神经网络的反向传播来调参数。你在左边画几个矩形当草图，右边的照片布局由一个小网络算出，它的 244 个参数随着你拖动实时训练。损失函数里加了一项对齐惩罚，照片会自己往一条线上靠，没有任何代码专门去对齐它们。参数很少，训练全在 JavaScript 里跑。

Cheng Lou 还设想，把一段 Handwired 程序接到 nanoGPT（Andrej Karpathy 的一个小型 GPT 训练项目）这样的模型上一起训练，模型既能写莎士比亚，又能精确执行那段程序。这个目前只是 README 里的设想，仓库里没有现成实现。

代码以 MIT 许可开源，demo 直接在网页上打开就能玩。想自己写，需要装 Bun，克隆仓库后从 template 目录的开关按钮示例开始，文档里有完整教程。

推文说“把普通 JS 代码变成神经网络”，容易让人以为能把现成代码丢进去自动转换。项目文档写的是：没有工具能把已有的 JavaScript 源码转成网络。你要用它提供的构建函数，把逻辑一句句写成比较、选择、加权求和这类操作。网络每次都要把所有操作跑一遍，不能提前退出，也不能跑运行时才知道次数的循环，所以常见的循环得改写成计数、树形合并之类的结构，文档专门用一章讲怎么改。所有数都是 32 位浮点数，每个值的取值范围要事先声明。

项目主页：https://chenglou.me/handwired/
GitHub：https://github.com/chenglou/handwired
原推文：https://x.com/_chenglou/status/2110557373651931267

text:
Engineering leaders told Grepr founder and CEO Jad Naous they spend 5 to 20% of their infrastructure budget on observability, and it's buying less and less reliability.

Jad, a former a16z partner, joins a16z's Martin Casado to discuss whether AI can run production systems as well as it writes code.

Grepr sits in a company's log stream, can scan a petabyte of logs a day, cuts observability costs by about 90%, and is building AI agents that use those signals to troubleshoot production issues.

How AI is changing engineering at Jad's 10-person company:
- A data lake feature that once took one engineer about six months took Jad 10 days
- The gap between okay and great engineers on his team "just multiplied 10X"
- He runs 3-4 agent sessions at once, with a "tech lead" agent reviewing every PR

Why running live systems is a harder problem for AI:
- Jad: AI can almost tune databases, but can't yet keep servers running on its own
- Martin: every bit of code doubles the ways a program can behave, which is why humans still own systems
- The real world is messier than AI's training data, self-driving took 20 years and $170B

@jadtnaous @grepr_ai @martin_casado

In 2022, Berkeley PhD student Woosuk Kwon thought he could make Meta's new open-weight model, OPT-175B, run faster in two weeks.

Four years and 3,000 contributors later, that project is @vllm_project, one of the largest open-source inference engines, running on ~500,000 GPUs at any given time.

He and fellow researchers Simon Mo, Kaichao You, and Roger Wang borrowed "virtual memory" from operating systems, handing out memory only as it's needed so each GPU can juggle requests of wildly different sizes. (The "v" in vLLM is for virtual.)

Their first user, Berkeley neighbor @arena, cut its GPU needs in half. Today Google, Amazon, and Meta all run vLLM in production.

In January, the core maintainers founded @inferact and raised $150M to give vLLM a full-time team.

They're hiring across eng, marketing, and devrel in SF and Singapore: https://a16zjobs.substack.com/p/inferact-raised-one-of-the-largest

@simon_mo_ @woosuk_k @KaichaoYou @rogerw0108

Jad Naous of @grepr_ai on how AI is widening the gap between okay and great engineers:

"Some people were adapting and learning and others weren't as adaptive. And then as we started hiring more people into the team, that disparity between okay engineers and really good engineers just multiplied 10X."

"Ultimately you really have to understand the setup. The more complexity that your brain can handle, the more you can break down the tasks and assign them."

"My team is still small... In my experience, for the things that we do, that is the case because we build distributed systems and distributed algorithms, and your brain has to handle the complexity because AI doesn't do it."

"For the problems that we solve, none of the models can actually think through the things that we do."

@jadtnaous @martin_casado
